papers.title: Manufacturing and characterization of similar to foam steel components processed through selective laser melting
papers.abstract: The growing interest from the industry for lightweight metal components has driven the development of processes that would allow creating lightweight high melting point metals as steels, able to guarantee mechanical characteristics superior to existing foam (typically aluminium), without penalizing one of the characteristics that cell structures have: lightness. Conventional manufacturing methods, such as casting, however, face difficulty in making complex periodic steel structures with designed shape and size and volume fraction. This study evaluates the manufacturability and performance of lightweight 17–4 PH steel components with spherical porosity fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM). Samples were designed and fabricated with the purpose to produce a structure similar to foam. Built samples were characterized in terms of dimensional accuracy, mechanical strength under compression and energy absorbed per unit mass. The designed structures have a designed relative density or volume fraction ranging between 31.1 and 32.8%.

summary_en.motivation: The paper aims to fabricate lightweight steel components with spherical porosity similar to metal foams using additive manufacturing.
summary_en.method: Samples with designed relative density of 31-33% were produced via selective laser melting and characterized for dimensional accuracy and compressive mechanical properties.
summary_en.result: The fabricated structures demonstrated good dimensional accuracy and high compressive strength and energy absorption per unit mass.
summary_en.validation: Mechanical compression testing was performed to evaluate strength and energy absorption.

papers.title: Laser beam melting 3D printing of Ti6Al4V based porous structured dental implants: fabrication, biocompatibility analysis and photoelastic study
papers.abstract: Fabricating Ti alloy based dental implants with defined porous scaffold structure is a promising strategy for improving the osteoinduction of implants. In this study, we use Laser Beam Melting (LBM) 3D printing technique to fabricate porous Ti6Al4V dental implant prototypes with three controlled pore sizes (200, 350 and 500 μm). The mechanical stress distribution in the surrounding bone tissue is characterized by photoelastography and associated finite element simulation. For in-vitro studies, experiments on implants' biocompatibility and osteogenic capability are conducted to evaluate the cellular response correlated to the porous structure. As the preliminary results, porous structured implants show a lower stress-shielding to the surrounding bone at the implant neck and a more densed distribution at the bottom site compared to the reference implant. From the cell proliferation tests and the immunofluorescence images, 350 and 500 μm pore sized implants demonstrate a better biocompatibility in terms of cell growth, migration and adhesion. Osteogenic genes expression of the 350 μm group is significantly increased alone with the ALP activity test. All these suggest that a pore size of 350 μm provides an optimal provides an optimal potential for improving the mechanical shielding to the surrounding bones and osteoinduction of the implant itself.

summary_zh.method: 采用激光束熔化3D打印制备三种孔径的多孔Ti6Al4V种植体，结合光弹性法和有限元分析力学性能。
summary_zh.result: 多孔种植体在颈部应力遮挡降低，350 μm孔径在细胞增殖和成骨基因表达方面最优。

summary_en.motivation: To improve osteoinduction and reduce stress shielding of dental implants through tailored porous structures.
summary_en.method: Laser beam melting (LBM) 3D printing was used to fabricate Ti6Al4V dental implants with three controlled pore sizes (200, 350, 500 μm), and mechanical stress distribution was analyzed using photoelastography and finite element simulation.
summary_en.result: Porous implants exhibited lower stress shielding at the implant neck and a denser stress distribution at the bottom compared to non-porous controls; the 350 μm pore size showed the best biocompatibility and osteogenic gene expression.
summary_en.validation: Mechanical validation was performed via photoelastography and finite element simulation, while biocompatibility was validated through in vitro cell proliferation, adhesion, and ALP activity assays.

papers.title: Mechanism of Hydrogen-Bonded Complex Formation between Ibuprofen and Nanocrystalline Hydroxyapatite.
papers.abstract: Nanocrystalline hydroxyapatite (nanoHA) is the main hard component of bone and has the potential to be used to promote osseointegration of implants and to treat bone defects. Here, using active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) such as ibuprofen, we report on the prospects of combining nanoHA with biologically active compounds to improve the clinical performance of these treatments. In this study, we designed and investigated the possibility of API attachment to the surface of nanoHA crystals via the formation of a hydrogen-bonded complex. The mechanistic studies of an ibuprofen/nanoHA complex formation have been performed using a holistic approach encompassing spectroscopic (Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) and Raman) and X-ray diffraction techniques, as well as quantum chemistry calculations, while comparing the behavior of the ibuprofen/nanoHA complex with that of a physical mixture of the two components. Whereas ibuprofen exists in dimeric form both in solid and liquid state, our study showed that the formation of the ibuprofen/nanoHA complex most likely occurs via the dissociation of the ibuprofen dimer into monomeric species promoted by ethanol, with subsequent attachment of a monomer to the HA surface. An adsorption mode for this process is proposed; this includes hydrogen bonding of the hydroxyl group of ibuprofen to the hydroxyl group of the apatite, together with the interaction of the ibuprofen carbonyl group to an HA Ca center. Overall, this mechanistic study provides new insights into the molecular interactions between APIs and the surfaces of bioactive inorganic solids and sheds light on the relationship between the noncovalent bonding and drug release properties.

summary_en.motivation: To understand the molecular interaction between ibuprofen and nanocrystalline hydroxyapatite for potential drug delivery applications.
summary_en.method: A combined approach using FTIR, Raman, X-ray diffraction, and quantum chemistry calculations was employed to study the complex formation.
summary_en.result: Ibuprofen adsorbs onto hydroxyapatite as monomers via hydrogen bonding with surface hydroxyl groups and coordination with calcium ions.
summary_en.validation: The proposed adsorption mode was supported by spectroscopic evidence and theoretical calculations.
